title: Is there a cheap way to wait and wake threads in Java?
body_excerpt: I am working on a concurrent problem where the critical section is not contested because every thread needs to have a go at some shared resource, but because some thread must, and there can be only one. Put simply, threads are happy to wait for anyone to finish the job, because (other than the cost of context switching) it does not slow them down, as otherwise they would have to do it themselves. This is not a once and done scenario; threads may require different 'levels of completion' of continuous work. The classic Java way of solving such a problem would be to acquire an object lock with [code] , check the state of protected variables, and go to sleep with [code] unless satisfied. Then, the thread doing the actual work periodically calls [code] to let them know about the progress being done. This is however not ideal, because each notified thread will sequentially need to acquire the lock and check the condition, even when they could all be awakened at once and do a volatile read of a variable completely concurrently. A second, somewhat related problem is that the cost of parking a thread is significant; are there lock implementations which optimistically try to spin lock for a bit in hopes that the resource will soon be available, before resorting to sleeping?

title: Ensuring the closed-world assumption when compiling GraalVM native images
body_excerpt: Recently I started playing around with GraalVM native images and immediately hit a snag. I was using Jackson to deserialize JSON data, and while the class parameter to [code] was a constant, the compiler still wasn't able to figure out that private fields of my class were needed for reflection, leading to an error at runtime. Now, this is an extremely simple lambda project, but I can't imagine the amount of possible, statically unverifiable errors I could get in a more complex project. In my opinion, this makes using libraries in native images useless, as you have no idea what needs to be accessed at runtime. It seems to me that the only way I can trust the compiled code is if I can verify that there are no dynamic reflection calls in the code that I'm using. So far, I haven't been able to find a way to do this. Worse yet, it seems like the GraalVM dashboard was removed from the internet, and the build report tool is not available in community edition JVMs. Even if I wanted to debug something by manually checking what's available for reflection in my image, I can't find a way to do it. As a side-question, I wonder if frameworks like Micronaut or Quarkus do anything to mitigate this problem.
